name: Esther Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. To start, could you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on the emergency housing desk at the Central Exchange benefits hub, right in the city centre. People come in who've been evicted or are sofa-surfing, and I process their emergency housing payment and the paperwork for a hostel or a temporary flat. It's fast and messy and I'm honestly still learning the rules for who counts as priority, so Owen, my team leader, reviews a lot of my decisions. I use the AI assistant all day to draft case notes, and I've built myself a little checklist bot for the priority rules.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I share a flat with Carla, who manages a cocktail bar, so our hours never match. At weekends I restore old furniture, chairs mostly, and sell them online. It's maybe two hundred a month extra, and it's the only time I'm not on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Huh. I'd be surprised, given how much I already use it. But okay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still worth using, it just isn't magic. I'd tell the team which prompts actually work so nobody wastes time on hype. Online I'd probably not say much, I'd be busy sanding a chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be fine. I'd have a steady job, a side income, and a bit saved. The only thing is the job itself is draining, so I'd be thinking about where I want to be at thirty, AI or no AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep using the assistant for case notes and share my priority-rules checklist with the desk. I'd keep the furniture going, maybe push it to three hundred a month. And I'd ask Owen about a move to the housing policy team in a couple of years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit restless. Not worried, just thinking about the next step.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's draining about the job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The stories. A woman with two kids in a car park, that kind of thing. I can draft a case note in two minutes with AI, but I still carry the car park home with me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Any money pressure?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. Rent is split with Carla, I've got about four months saved and the chairs pay for my phone and fun. If anything, I'm a bit too relaxed about pensions.

I'd share the **prompts that work** so colleagues skip the hype.

The job is **draining**, so I'm thinking about where I'll be at thirty.

Grow the **furniture sales** to about three hundred a month.
Ask my team leader about the **housing policy team**.
feel: **Calm** but a bit **restless** about her next step.

fieldNote: She is a **daily AI user** who builds her own small tools.

Grow weekend chair restoration sales to three hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I believe. It's already half happening on my desk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and we should get ahead of it, not pretend. Use it for the paperwork and give caseworkers more time with people. I'd probably say that at a team meeting and get a few eye rolls.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think the emergency desk shrinks but doesn't vanish, because people walk in crying and someone has to deal with that. The juniors who only do paperwork go. I'd want to be the person who sets up and checks the tools, which is a small team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd volunteer for the hub's AI rollout, write the guidance, run sessions. I'd apply for the department's digital operations jobs. And I'd look at the claims-software firms that sell to councils, because they'd be hiring people who know the work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but more curious than worried. Change is easier to handle if you're in the room for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave public service for a software firm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, if the pay was better. I'm in the middle on that stuff. I like public service, but I'm not going to stay loyal to a desk that's being quietly turned into software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen, actually. He's brilliant at the rules and terrible with computers. He's forty-five with two kids. I'd try to teach him the tools on the quiet.

I'd argue it should free **caseworker time** for people.

I'd aim to **set up and check** the tools on a small team.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years is tight. Even for me, and I like this stuff.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we need a safety net fast: income support while people retrain, and quick. I'd say it to everyone, including the people who think I'm an AI cheerleader.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my caseworker job goes by 2028, along with the digital operations job I'd been eyeing, because AGI does that too. The thing I've got is the furniture. It's hands-on, so I'd have until about 2031 before robots, and people may still want a human-made chair after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd turn the furniture into a real business, rent a small workshop unit and take on commissions. I'd keep the caseworker job as long as it lasted, but stop putting effort into promotion. And I'd move savings to six months by cutting going out with Carla.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. Excited too, which feels wrong to say. But mostly anxious, because a workshop is a risk.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the workshop cost?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: About three hundred a month for a unit by the canal, plus tools, maybe a thousand to start. I'd spend a thousand on tools and a workshop by the canal, because sanding a chair is the one thing in my life a computer can't do yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the chairs don't sell?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I've lost a thousand and learned something. I've got four months saved. I'd rather fail trying than wait at a desk for a letter.

say: I'd demand a **fast safety net** with income support during retraining.
I'd say it to everyone, even those who see me as an **AI cheerleader**.
think: My caseworker job and **digital roles** would both go by 2028.
My **furniture work** is hands-on and lasts until robots around 2031.

fieldNote: She uses the **robot gap** directly by building up hands-on work.

She is **willing to risk** a thousand on her own business.

steps.text: Rent a workshop unit by the canal for about three hundred a month

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's about the time it takes to build a small business properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is enough to retrain people if the government starts now, and enough for people to start things. I'd tell friends to get a skill that needs their hands.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my caseworker job goes around 2031, so I'd plan to be out before then. I'd do the digital operations job for two or three years, for the money and the experience, then go full time on furniture before the robots get good, around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take the digital operations job if I got it, and save the difference in pay. I'd do a short upholstery course at the college on Thursday evenings. And I'd set up the workshop in year three, with savings to cover six months of slow sales.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, but in a planning way. Five years feels like a project plan with a deadline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does it worry you that robots come for the furniture too, around 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yes, a bit. But a robot restoring someone's grandmother's chair? People pay for the story. A factory robot can make a thousand chairs, but people will still pay me to fix their grandmother's chair.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does Carla think?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: She thinks I'm mad, in a nice way. She says she'll put my chairs in the bar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years is a long runway. I'd treat that as a gift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've been given time, so let's not waste it arguing. Plan the retraining, protect people, and let folks experiment. I'd probably say it a bit too cheerfully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd do well. I'd have years in the digital team, a growing furniture business, and savings. The end point still takes my desk work, but I'd have moved on by then, and the hands-on bit lasts till about 2039.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go for the housing policy team, then digital. I'd grow the furniture slowly and put some of the money into a pension, which I've been ignoring. And I'd learn every new AI tool for the business side, pricing and listings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly good. Ten years is enough to be someone else by the end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there a catch you're not seeing?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably that everyone else gets the same idea. If ten years of warning makes everyone take up a craft, I'll be one of a million people selling restored chairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Find a niche. Office chairs for the old council buildings, maybe. I'd use the AI to find the buyers.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028. My furniture plan needs a few years and two isn't enough. What would help is income support while you retrain, and cheap workshop space from the council for people starting hands-on work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe the people we serve. The people coming to my desk after an eviction don't have a side business or four months saved, and they'd be hit first.

headlineQuote: The people coming to my desk after an eviction don't have a side business or four months saved, and they'd be hit first.
portrait: Esther is a **27-year-old** junior emergency housing caseworker in a city-centre benefits hub.
She uses AI **every day**, builds her own small tools, and restores furniture at weekends.
She stays **calm** in AI Plateau and reaches **anxious** in the faster AGI pictures.
She plans to ride both waves: **digital work** first, then a hands-on **furniture business**.
She is pragmatic, **open to leaving** public service, and worried for vulnerable claimants.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, giving too little time to build the furniture business.
whatWouldHelp: Cheap **council workshop space** for people starting hands-on work.
